title: The ENTIRE History of the Persian Empire in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of the Persian Empire in 10 Minutes (550 BC–651 AD)
description:
From Cyrus the Great to the Arab conquest, this is the whole story of the Persian empires from 550 BC to 651 AD in about ten minutes: Croesus and the oracle, Cambyses in Egypt, Darius and the Royal Road, Xerxes and the Greeks, Alexander burning Persepolis, the Parthian shot, Shapur capturing a Roman emperor, and the last Sasanian king. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #persia #persianempire #ancienthistory #animatedhistory

beats.say: 330 BC. Alexander the Great is partying inside the most magnificent palace on Earth.
It belongs to the king of Persia, whose empire Alexander has just smashed.
Nice palace. It would be a shame if something happened to it.
Boss? Why are you holding a torch?
By morning, the great palace of Persepolis was a smoking ruin.
Ancient writers called it revenge, because the Persians had burned Athens a hundred and fifty years earlier.
So how did Persia get so big that Alexander wanted to burn it? Let's go back to the beginning.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of the Persian Empire in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From Cyrus to the Arab conquest, 550 BC to 651 AD

beats.say: Around 550 BC, Persia was a small kingdom in what is now southern Iran.
Its king, Cyrus, had to answer to a bigger neighbor, the kingdom of the Medes.

tag.text: Cyrus the Great, king of Persia

beats.say: So Cyrus rebelled, beat the Medes, and took their whole kingdom. Talk about a promotion.
Next door was Lydia, in what is now Turkey. Its king, Croesus, was one of the richest men alive.
Croesus asked the oracle at Delphi, a Greek priestess who gave advice from the gods, whether to attack Persia.
If you attack Persia, you will destroy a great empire.
A great empire? Sounds great. Pack the chariots!
He did destroy a great empire, says Herodotus, the Greek historian. His own. Cyrus took his capital, Sardis.
In 539 BC Cyrus went after Babylon, the giant city of Mesopotamia. Its gates opened without a fight.
Cyrus didn't wipe out the people he conquered. He kept their local customs and gods, so fewer of them wanted to rebel.
The Bible remembers Cyrus for letting the Jews who had been taken to Babylon go home to Jerusalem.
He also had a clay cylinder made, bragging that the gods chose him. Today it sits in the British Museum.
Some people call it the first human rights charter. Most historians say that's a stretch: it's mostly royal bragging.
Most accounts say Cyrus died in battle in 530 BC, fighting nomads in Central Asia. He left his son a brand-new superpower.
That son, Cambyses, wanted the one prize Dad never got: Egypt.
In 525 BC he beat the Egyptian army at Pelusium, on the edge of the Nile delta.
Egypt became a Persian province, and the pharaoh's land now answered to a king in Persia.
Herodotus also tells a spooky story: Cambyses sent fifty thousand men across the desert, and a sandstorm swallowed them.
Herodotus was only repeating what locals told him, and no one has ever found that army. Most historians call it a legend.
In 522 BC, Cambyses died on the way home. Suddenly the biggest empire in the world had no clear boss.
Enter Darius, a young Persian noble who grabbed the throne with six friends.
He said the man he overthrew was a fake, pretending to be Cyrus's son. Some historians suspect Darius made that up.
He even carved his version high up a cliff at Behistun, in three languages, so nobody could miss it.
Then he got organized. He split the empire into provinces called satrapies, each run by a governor.
His empire ran from Egypt to the edge of India. Nobody had ever ruled so much of the world.
He also made gold coins called darics, so people could pay for things almost anywhere in the empire.
He also improved the Royal Road, about twenty-seven hundred kilometers from Sardis in the west to Susa.
On foot, the trip took about three months. Royal riders did it in about a week.

show.label: The Royal Road, Sardis to Susa
show.sub: about 1,700 miles: 90 days on foot, about 7 to 9 days by relay riders

beats.say: The trick was relay stations. Each rider galloped one day's stretch, then handed the message to a fresh rider.
Message for the king! Your turn. Go, go, go!
Got it. You go take a nap.
Herodotus was so impressed that his words about them ended up carved on New York's main post office.

show.text: Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift completion of their appointed rounds.
show.who: Herodotus, Histories 8.98, as carved on the James A. Farley Post Office in New York

beats.say: Darius also built Persepolis, a giant palace city. Its clay records show workers were paid in food, and new mothers got extra.
Persians were clever with water, too. They dug qanats, underground canals that carry mountain water to desert farms using only gravity.
Some qanats in Iran still carry water today, and UNESCO lists them as World Heritage.
Greek cities on Persia's western coast rebelled, and Athens sent ships to help them. Darius took that personally.
In 490 BC his army landed near Athens. The Athenians beat it at the Battle of Marathon.
Darius died before he could try again. In 480 BC his son Xerxes came back with a far bigger army.
When a storm wrecked his bridge of boats, Herodotus says Xerxes had the sea whipped. The sea did not apologize.
His elite guard were the Immortals. Herodotus says any man lost was replaced at once, so there were always ten thousand.
Xerxes won at Thermopylae and burned Athens. Then the Greek fleet trapped his ships at Salamis and smashed them.
A year later the Greeks won again at Plataea. Persia gave up on conquering Greece, but the empire itself was fine.
Then in 334 BC, a twenty-one-year-old king from Macedonia, north of Greece, invaded Persia.
He won at the Granicus River, then at Issus, then at Gaugamela, in what is now northern Iraq.
At Issus, the Persian king, Darius the Third, ran away so fast he left his own family behind.
Darius offered a huge deal: land, gold, and his daughter in marriage. Alexander's top general liked it.
If I were Alexander, I would take it.
So would I, if I were Parmenion.
That comeback comes from ancient writers like Plutarch and Arrian. Alexander wanted all of Persia.
After Gaugamela came the fire at Persepolis. Then in 330 BC, Darius was killed by his own nobles while on the run.
Alexander gave Darius a royal funeral. Then he started wearing Persian royal clothes himself.
The first Persian Empire was over.

show.label: The first Persian Empire lasted about

beats.say: Alexander died young, and his generals split his empire. Greek kings ruled Persia for a while.
Then, around 247 BC, nomad horsemen from east of the Caspian Sea took over. They became the Parthians.
Their signature move was the Parthian shot: gallop away, twist around in the saddle, and shoot backward.
Parthia also sat in the middle of the Silk Road, the trade routes between China and Rome, and got rich taxing the traffic.
Some say that's where the phrase parting shot comes from, though word experts still argue about it.
In 53 BC, at Carrhae, the Parthians wiped out a Roman army. Rome and Parthia stayed bitter rivals for centuries.
In 224 AD, a Persian noble named Ardashir beat the last Parthian king and started a new family of kings: the Sasanians.
The Sasanians built huge palaces with giant brick arches, and made Zoroastrianism, an old Persian religion, the official faith.
His son, Shapur the First, fought Rome. In 260 AD, near Edessa, he did something no one had ever done.
I am the emperor of Rome! Release me at once!
Relax. You're my guest now. Forever.
Shapur captured Emperor Valerian. He was the first Roman emperor ever taken prisoner, and he died in Persia.
Shapur had giant pictures of defeated Roman emperors carved into rock cliffs. Just to make sure nobody forgot.
Rome and Persia kept fighting for four hundred years. The last big war, from 602 to 628, left both empires exhausted and broke.
Then a new power burst out of Arabia: the armies of the first Muslim caliphs, the leaders who came after Muhammad.
They beat the Persians at Qadisiyyah around 636, then again at Nahavand in 642.
The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd the Third, fled east from city to city.
In 651 he was killed near Merv, in what is now Turkmenistan. The age of the Persian empires was over.
But Persian culture didn't disappear. Its language, its poetry and its new-year festival, Nowruz, are still alive today.
Around the year 1010, the poet Ferdowsi finished the Book of Kings, a giant poem in Persian about the old kings and heroes.
So that's Persia: a small kingdom that built a superpower, and Persian empires that rose and fell for about twelve hundred years.
